Bayesian Sheaf Neural Networks

Patrick Gillespie Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN, USA Email: pgilles5@vols.utk.edu    Layal Bou Hamdan Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN, USA Email: lbouhamd@vols.utk.edu    Ioannis Schizas Affiliation: DEVCOM ARL, Army Research Lab, Aberdeen, MD, USA Email: ioannis.d.schizas.civ@army.mil    David L. Boothe Affiliation: DEVCOM ARL, Army Research Lab, Aberdeen, MD, USA Email:  david.l.boothe7.civ@army.mil    Vasileios Maroulas Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN, USA Email: vasileios.maroulas@utk.edu

Abstract

Equipping graph neural networks with a convolution operation defined in terms of a cellular sheaf offers advantages for learning expressive representations of heterophilic graph data. The most flexible approach to constructing the sheaf is to learn it as part of the network as a function of the node features. However, this leaves the network potentially overly sensitive to the learned sheaf. As a counter-measure, we propose a variational approach to learning cellular sheaves within sheaf neural networks, yielding an architecture we refer to as a Bayesian sheaf neural network. As part of this work, we define a novel family of reparameterizable probability distributions on the rotation group S​O​(n)SO(n) using the Cayley transform. We evaluate the Bayesian sheaf neural network on several graph datasets, and show that our Bayesian sheaf models achieve leading performance compared to baseline models and are less sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters under limited training data settings.

Keywords: Cellular sheaf, Bayesian neural network, variational inference, Cayley transform, uncertainty quantification.

1 Introduction

Geometric and topological deep learning are rapidly developing research areas which, broadly speaking, aim to use geometric priors about the data of interest to develop neural network architectures using methods and tools from differential geometry, topology, and graph theory [14, 55]. Graph neural networks are a central method in geometric deep learning and have been applied to a wide range of tasks such as recommender systems [64], traffic modeling [51, 65], and predicting properties of chemicals [35]. Building on the basic idea of graph neural networks, architectures such as simplicial and hypergraph neural networks extend the graph convolutions to higher-order operations, which have advantages when the dataset contains salient relationships among groups of nodes rather than just node pairs, as in citation networks [26, 30], chemical data [9, 8], and neural data [53]. However, such convolution operators suffer from over-smoothing, and thus tend to perform best on homophilic graph data, where connected nodes have a high likelihood of belonging to the same class [59, 10].

Several approaches have been taken to address the limited capabilities of GCNs and higher-order variants for heterophilic graph data (i.e., not homophilic) [63, 57, 69, 67]. One approach replaces the graph convolution operation with one defined in terms of a cellular sheaf [40, 10]. A cellular sheaf on a graph assigns a vector space to each vertex and each edge, along with linear maps, known as restriction maps, that relate the data on edges to the data on their incident vertices. Restriction maps provide additional flexibility in the message passing operation. They allow neighboring nodes to maintain distinct features throughout the layers of the sheaf neural network: an advantageous quality when working with heterophilic graph data.

While sheaf neural networks were developed to address the issue of over-smoothing in graph neural networks, they are still susceptible to many of the issues common to all neural networks, such as overfitting to limited training data and lack of robustness to noisy data, weight initializations, and hyperparameter selections. An approach to mitigating such issues is to apply tools and ideas from Bayesian statistics to deep learning [44, 56]. Bayesian approaches to machine learning have been used to quantify the uncertainty in neural network predictions [46, 33], reduce overfitting [32, 34], add robustness to adversarial attacks [11], and to improve the overall predictive performance of machine learning algorithms [28, 37, 52].

In this paper, we apply a Bayesian framework to learning cellular sheaves within a sheaf neural network. Specifically, we consider the sheaf Laplacian as an object that enables the integration of the graph Laplacian with cellular sheaves, treating it as a latent random variable of the sheaf neural network.

Our main contributions are as follows.

  1. 1.

    We introduce Bayesian sheaf neural networks (BSNN) in which the sheaf Laplacian operator of the sheaf neural network is a latent random variable whose distribution is parameterized by a function of the input data. Motivated by the evidence lower bound for variational Bayesian inference, we derive a pertinent loss function for our BSNN which contains a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence regularization term, enabling efficient training.

  2. 2.

    We define a novel family of reparameterizable probability distributions on the rotation group S​O​(n)SO(n) that we refer to as Cayley distributions. The Cayley distributions are reparameterizable and have tractable density functions, and thus can be used to perform variational inference on the sheaf Laplacian within the BSNN when the sheaf restriction maps belong to S​O​(n)SO(n). We derive closed-form expressions for the KL divergence of the Cayley distributions from the uniform distribution on S​O​(n)SO(n) when n=2,3n=2,3.

  3. 3.

    We incorporate uncertainty quantification to rigorously evaluate our BSNN models on several benchmark graph datasets for node classification tasks, presenting extensive numerical results and comprehensive sensitivity analyses to validate robustness and performance.

1.1 Related Work

We first discuss existing work on sheaf neural networks. Sheaf neural networks (SNN) were first introduced by [40], where they were shown to outperform graph convolutional networks on a semi-supervised node classification task using a hand-selected cellular sheaf. A more in-depth investigation of sheaf neural networks, sheaf diffusion processes, and the advantage of SNNs for heterophilic graph data was performed in [10], where they also constructed a method of learning a suitable cellular sheaf from the data as part of the sheaf neural network.

Building on these foundational approaches, several variants of SNNs have been proposed that extend their applicability or enhance their expressiveness. They include SNNs with attention-based edge weights [4] and SNNs defined for hypergraphs rather than cellular complexes [25]. In addition to hand-crafting a sheaf for a particular problem or learning a sheaf during training, [3] construct a sheaf at preprocessing time by assuming the graph data lie on a low-dimensional manifold and defining a cellular sheaf in a manner inspired by connections from differential geometry.

While SNNs have not yet been explored through a Bayesian lens, uncertainty modeling and probabilistic reasoning have played an increasing role in geometric deep learning more broadly. A variational auto-encoder using graph convolutional layers was considered in [48] for an edge detection task. [23] discuss variational auto-encoders where the latent variable takes values in a hypersphere. [37] combine graph variational autoencoders with graph recurrent networks to outperform existing state-of-the-art methods on dynamic link prediction tasks. Beyond variational autoencoders, [28] model attention weights in graph attention networks as random latent variables, as well as in other architectures which use attention. Given that the inclusion or exclusion of edges in graph datasets can be due to spurious noise or modeling assumptions, [66] view graph datasets as realizations of parametric families of random graphs, and develop a Bayesian graph convolutional network accordingly.

A key component of a Bayesian formulation for sheaf neural networks is defining a distribution over the space of restriction maps, which often lie in the special orthogonal S​O​(n)SO(n). The most well-known probability distributions on S​O​(n)SO(n) are the matrix Langevin (or von Mises-Fisher) distribution [54, 19] and the matrix Bingham distribution [18]. However, such distributions are not easily reparameterizable, which makes incorporating them within neural networks trained via backpropagation difficult. While the matrix exponential used by [27] provides a reparameterizable mapping to S​O​(d)SO(d), it lacks tractable densities.

In this paper, we define a family of reparameterizable distributions on S​O​(n)SO(n) using the Cayley transform which we refer to as Cayley distributions. These are distinct from the Cayley distributions defined in [50], and we compare the two families of distributions in Section 3.3. Moreover, [43] used a generalized version of the Cayley transform to simulate distributions on Stiefel and Grassmann manifolds, illustrating the broader applicability of Cayley-type methods in geometric statistics.

1.2 Overview

In Section 2, we review preliminary topics such as cellular sheaves and sheaf Laplacians. We review how the sheaf Laplacian can be used to define a sheaf neural network, and the connection to a sheaf diffusion process. We also review the Cayley distribution, variational inference, and several uncertainty quantification metrics. In Section 3, we describe our variational approach to learning cellular sheaves in a sheaf neural network. We prove a result regarding the linear separation power of a sheaf diffusion process for sheaves consisting of special orthogonal maps. We define a reparameterizable family of distributions on S​O​(n)SO(n), which is used to define the variational distribution for cellular sheaves with special orthogonal restriction maps. In Section 4, we evaluate our BSNN models on several node classification tasks and measure their predictive uncertainty. We end with a final discussion, as well as potential directions for future work in Section 5.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Cellular Sheaves over Graphs

Definition 1.

A cellular sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} on an undirected graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) assigns a vector space ℱ⁡(v)\mathcal{F}(v) to each node v∈Vv\in V, a vector space ℱ⁡(e)\mathcal{F}(e) to each edge e∈Ee\in E, and a linear map ℱv​⊴​e:ℱ⁡(v)→ℱ⁡(e)\mathcal{F}_{v\trianglelefteq e}:\mathcal{F}(v)\to\mathcal{F}(e) for each incident pair v​⊴​ev\trianglelefteq e (i.e., node vv is incident to edge ee).

Remark 1.

In the language of sheaf theory, ℱ⁡(v)\mathcal{F}(v) is called the stalk over vv, and ℱv​⊴​e\mathcal{F}_{v\trianglelefteq e} is called a restriction map [13].

Definition 2.

The spaces of 00-cochains and 11-cochains are defined as the direct sums

C0​(G,ℱ):=⨁v∈Vℱ⁡(v)andC1​(G,ℱ):=⨁e∈Eℱ⁡(e),C^{0}(G;\mathcal{F}):=\bigoplus_{v\in V}\mathcal{F}(v)\quad\text{and}\quad C^{1}(G;\mathcal{F}):=\bigoplus_{e\in E}\mathcal{F}(e),

corresponding to the vector spaces assigned to the nodes and edges, respectively.

Definition 3.

Let x∈C0​(G,ℱ)x\in C^{0}(G;\mathcal{F}), xvx_{v} denotes the value of xx at ℱ⁡(v)\mathcal{F}(v). The coboundary map δ:C0​(G,ℱ)→C1​(G,ℱ)\delta:C^{0}(G;\mathcal{F})\to C^{1}(G;\mathcal{F}) is defined componentwise by

(δ​x)e=ℱv​⊴​e​(xv)−ℱu​⊴​e​(xu),(\delta x)_{e}=\mathcal{F}_{v\trianglelefteq e}(x_{v})-\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}(x_{u}),

where ee is an edge oriented from uu to vv (this orientation is chosen arbitrarily to define a consistent sign convention; the graph itself remains undirected).

Definition 4.

The sheaf Laplacian Lℱ:C0​(G,ℱ)→C0​(G,ℱ)L_{\mathcal{F}}:C^{0}(G;\mathcal{F})\to C^{0}(G;\mathcal{F}) is defined as

Lℱ:=δ⊤​δ.L_{\mathcal{F}}:=\delta^{\top}\delta.

Given a sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} on a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) with nn nodes, and assuming that the stalk ℱ⁡(u)\mathcal{F}(u) over each node u∈Vu\in V has the same dimension dd, the sheaf Laplacian LℱL_{\mathcal{F}} can be represented as a block matrix of size n​d×n​dnd\times nd. The off-diagonal blocks Li​j∈ℝd×dL_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} are given by Li​j=−ℱuj​⊴​e⊤​ℱui​⊴​e​ if there exists an edge ​e​ between nodes ​ui​ and ​uj,L_{ij}=-\mathcal{F}_{u_{j}\trianglelefteq e}^{\top}\mathcal{F}_{u_{i}\trianglelefteq e}\text{ if there exists an edge }e\text{ between nodes }u_{i}\text{ and }u_{j}, and 00 otherwise. The diagonal blocks are given by Li​i=∑ui​⊴​eℱui​⊴​e⊤​ℱui​⊴​e,L_{ii}=\sum_{u_{i}\trianglelefteq e}\mathcal{F}_{u_{i}\trianglelefteq e}^{\top}\mathcal{F}_{u_{i}\trianglelefteq e}, where the sum is taken over all edges ee incident to uiu_{i}.

Remark 2.

Analogously to how message passing in graph convolutional networks uses the graph Laplacian L=D−AL=D-A [48], the sheaf Laplacian LℱL_{\mathcal{F}} defines message passing on cellular sheaves. For further information on cellular sheaves and sheaf Laplacians, we refer the interested reader to [39].

Definition 5.

The normalized 00th sheaf Laplacian Δℱ\Delta_{\mathcal{F}} associated with a cellular sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} over a graph GG is defined as

Δℱ:=D−1/2LℱD−1/2,\Delta_{\mathcal{F}}:=D^{-1/2}L_{\mathcal{F}}D^{-1/2},

where DD is the block-diagonal matrix whose diagonal blocks are the Li​iL_{ii} and whose off-diagonal blocks are zero matrices [40].

Remark 3.

The matrix DD is symmetric positive semi-definite, and therefore there exists a matrix D1/2D^{1/2} such that D1/2​D1/2=DD^{1/2}D^{1/2}=D. 2.2 Sheaf Diffusion

Let GG be a graph with nn nodes and with dd−-dimensional node features, and let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a cellular sheaf over GG with dd−-dimensional stalks. We represent the node features as an n​dnd−-dimensional vector X∈ℝn​dX\in\mathbb{R}^{nd} so that the normalized sheaf Laplacian Δℱ\Delta_{\mathcal{F}}, as an n​d×n​dnd\times nd block matrix, updates XX by matrix-vector multiplication Δℱ​X\Delta_{\mathcal{F}}X. Motivated by how the graph convolutional layers of [48] can be viewed as a discretization of a heat diffusion process dd​t​X​(t)=−Δ​X​(t)\tfrac{d}{dt}X(t)=-\Delta X(t) defined in terms of the normalized graph Laplacian Δ\Delta, a similar diffusion process uses the sheaf Laplacian:

X⁡(0)=X,dd​t​X​(t)=−Δℱ​X​(t).X(0)=X,\quad\tfrac{d}{dt}X(t)=-\Delta_{\mathcal{F}}X(t). (1)

Applying the Euler method with unit time-steps to approximate solutions to Eq.(1) yields

X⁡(t+1)=X⁡(t)−Δℱ​X​(t).X(t+1)=X(t)-\Delta_{\mathcal{F}}X(t). (2)

The authors of [10] use Eq.(2) to define sheaf diffusion layers as follows. Allowing for f∈ℕf\in\mathbb{N} distinct feature channels, let X∈ℝn​d×fX\in\mathbb{R}^{nd\times f} be a feature matrix. Given a sheaf Laplacian operator Δℱ⁡(t)\Delta_{\mathcal{F}(t)} for layer tt, a sheaf diffusion layer is defined by setting

Xt+1=Xt−σ⁡(Δℱ⁡(t)​(In⊗Wt,1)​Xt​Wt,2).X_{t+1}=X_{t}-\sigma\big(\Delta_{\mathcal{F}(t)}(I_{n}\otimes W_{t,1})X_{t}W_{t,2}\big). (3)

Here Wt,1∈ℝd×dW_{t,1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} and Wt,2∈ℝf×fW_{t,2}\in\mathbb{R}^{f\times f} are weight matrices for layer tt, σ\sigma is a nonlinear activation function, ⊗\otimes denotes a Kronecker product.

As a measure of the expressive power of the sheaf layers based on Eq.(2), [10] study the ability of the sheaf diffusion process in Eq.(1) to linearly separate the features of nodes belonging to different classes.

Definition 6.

A class of sheaves ℋd\mathcal{H}^{d} with dd−-dimensional stalks is said to have linear separation power over a class of labeled graphs 𝒢\mathcal{G} if for every G∈𝒢G\in\mathcal{G}, there exists a sheaf ℱ∈ℋd\mathcal{F}\in\mathcal{H}^{d} such that the sheaf diffusion process determined by ℱ\mathcal{F} on GG linearly separates the features X⁡(t)X(t) of the classes of GG in the time limit t→∞t\to\infty, for almost all initial conditions X⁡(0)X(0).

As part of a sheaf learning mechanism within a sheaf neural network, a fixed class of sheaves ℋd\mathcal{H}^{d} is parameterized, and the input data is mapped to a suitable sheaf ℱ∈ℋd\mathcal{F}\in\mathcal{H}^{d} through this parameterization.

For a node classification task with CC classes, the collection of sheaves ℋd\mathcal{H}^{d} should ideally have linear separation power over the collection of connected graphs with CC classes. While one could always take ℋd\mathcal{H}^{d} to be as general as possible, learning cellular sheaves whose restriction maps are diagonal or special orthogonal matrices involves fewer parameters. Recall that a special orthogonal matrix, that is, an element of S​O​(n)SO(n), is a matrix QQ such that QT=Q−1Q^{T}=Q^{-1} and det(Q)=1\det(Q)=1.

The class of sheaves ℋdiagd\mathcal{H}^{d}_{\diag} with invertible diagonal restriction maps was shown to have linear separation power over the collection 𝒢C\mathcal{G}_{C} of connected graphs with CC classes whenever C≤dC\leq d [10]. However, for ℋs​od\mathcal{H}_{so}^{d}, the class of sheaves with d×dd\times d special orthogonal restriction maps, as discussed in Proposition 13 of [10], only guarantees the existence of a dd such that ℋs​od\mathcal{H}_{so}^{d} has linear separation power over 𝒢C\mathcal{G}_{C} when C≤8C\leq 8.

Remark 4.

Although [10] consider sheaves with orthogonal restriction maps (i.e., elements of the orthogonal group O⁡(n)O(n)), the sheaf learning mechanism in their SNN is a continuous parametrization of O⁡(n)O(n) by the connected space ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m}, so it must have its image contained in a connected component of O⁡(n)O(n). This implies that the restriction maps ℱu​⊴​e\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e} will either all have determinant 11 or all have determinant −1-1. The maps ℱu​⊴​e𝖳​ℱv​⊴​e\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathcal{F}_{v\trianglelefteq e} used in the sheaf Laplacian must always have a determinant equal to 11. Thus, it is effectively equivalent to learning restriction maps belonging to the special orthogonal group S​O​(n)SO(n).

2.3 Cayley Transform

Definition 7.

We denote the set of all n×nn\times n skew-symmetric matrices by 𝔰​𝔬​(n)\mathfrak{so}(n). The Cayley transform[15] is a function C:𝔰​𝔬​(n)→S​O​(n)C:\mathfrak{so}(n)\to SO(n) defined by

C⁡(A)=(I−A)−1​(I+A)=2​(I−A)−1−I.C(A)=(I-A)^{-1}(I+A)=2(I-A)^{-1}-I. (4)

If AA is an n×nn\times n skew-symmetric matrix, then x𝖳​A​x=0x^{\mathsf{T}}Ax=0 for all x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n} due to the fact that x𝖳​A​x=(x𝖳​A​x)𝖳=−x𝖳​A​xx^{\mathsf{T}}Ax=(x^{\mathsf{T}}Ax)^{\mathsf{T}}=-x^{\mathsf{T}}Ax. Hence, if (I−A)​x=0(I-A)x=0, then x𝖳​(I−A)​x=x𝖳​x=0x^{\mathsf{T}}(I-A)x=x^{\mathsf{T}}x=0 implies that x=0x=0. Thus, I−AI-A is invertible, showing that the Cayley transform is well-defined. If P∈S​O​(n)P\in SO(n) does not have −1-1 as an eigenvalue, C−1​(P)C^{-1}(P) exists and is given by

C−1​(P)=(P−I)​(I+P)−1=I−2​(I+P)−1.C^{-1}(P)=(P-I)(I+P)^{-1}=I-2(I+P)^{-1}. (5)

Hence CC is injective, and all but a measure zero subset of S​O​(n)SO(n) is contained in the image of CC.

The Cayley transform is sometimes alternatively defined as C⁡(A)=(I+A)−1​(I−A)=(I−A)​(I+A)−1C(A)=(I+A)^{-1}(I-A)=(I-A)(I+A)^{-1}. Since the two definitions differ only by the precomposition of CC with the reflection A↦−AA\mapsto-A, either choice of definition could be used without meaningful change.

For a vector ϕ∈ℝn⁡(n−1)/2\phi\in\mathbb{R}^{n(n-1)/2}, let XϕX_{\phi} denote the skew symmetric matrix containing the entries of ϕ\phi as its lower triangular entries. Explicitly, if ϕ=(ϕ1,ϕ2,…,ϕn⁡(n−1)/2)\phi=(\phi_{1},\phi_{2},\dots,\phi_{n(n-1)/2}) and if xi​jx_{ij} denotes the i,ji,j−-th entry of XϕX_{\phi}, then for i>ji>j, set xi​j=−xj​i=ϕi​j−j⁡(j+1)/2x_{ij}=-x_{ji}=\phi_{ij-j(j+1)/2} and set xi​i=0x_{ii}=0. The Jacobian (determinant) of C~\widetilde{C} is J​C~​(ϕ)=det(D​C~​(ϕ)𝖳​D​C~​(ϕ))1/2J\widetilde{C}(\phi)=\det(D\widetilde{C}(\phi)^{\mathsf{T}}D\widetilde{C}(\phi))^{1/2}, where D​C~​(ϕ)D\widetilde{C}(\phi) denotes the total derivative of C~\widetilde{C} at the point ϕ\phi. J​C~​(ϕ)=23​n​(n−1)/4det(I+Xϕ)n−1.J\widetilde{C}(\phi)=\frac{2^{3n(n-1)/4}}{\det(I+X_{\phi})^{n-1}}. (6)

2.4 Variational Inference

Let PP be a distribution on a measurable space 𝒳\mathcal{X} with density pp with respect to some reference measure μ\mu. If XX is a random variable with distribution PP, we write X∼PX\sim P. To simplify notation, we will often refer to a distribution by its density function.

For a function f:𝒳→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}, we denote by 𝔼P​[f​(X)]\mathbb{E}_{P}[f(X)] the expectation of f⁡(X)f(X) with respect to PP, that is,

𝔼P​[f⁡(X)]=∫𝒳p⁡(x)​f​(x)​μ​(𝑑x).\mathbb{E}_{P}[f(X)]=\int_{\mathcal{X}}p(x)f(x)\,\mu(dx). (7)

The Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence is a fundamental measure from information theory that quantifies how one probability distribution diverges from a second, reference distribution [21]. If QQ is another distribution over 𝒳\mathcal{X} with density qq (also with respect to μ\mu), the KL divergence of PP from QQ is defined as

KL(P∥Q)=∫𝒳p(x)log(p⁡(x)q⁡(x))μ(dx).\mathrm{KL}(P\,\|\,Q)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}p(x)\log\left(\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\right)\mu(dx). (8)

Variational Inference (VI) transforms the problem of approximating intractable posterior distributions into an optimization task. Given a latent variable model with observations yy and latent variables zz, the posterior p⁡(z|y)p(z|y) is often intractable due to the marginal likelihood requiring integration over the latent space. VI addresses this challenge by introducing a family of tractable distributions qϕ​(z){q_{\phi}(z)}, parameterized by variational parameters ϕ\phi, and finding the member of this family that is closest to the true posterior in terms of the KL divergence:

ϕ∗=argminϕKL(qϕ(z)∥p(z∣y)).\phi^{*}=\arg\min_{\phi}\operatorname{KL}\left(q_{\phi}(z)\|p(z\mid y)\right). (9)

This optimization is equivalent to maximizing the evidence lower bound (ELBO), which provides a lower bound on the marginal log-likelihood log⁡p⁡(y)\log p(y). The ELBO is given by

ℒ⁡(ϕ)=𝔼qϕ​(z)​[log⁡p⁡(y,z)]−𝔼qϕ​(z)​[log⁡qϕ​(z)].\mathcal{L}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(z)}[\log p(y,z)]-\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(z)}\left[\log q_{\phi}(z)\right]. (10)

Intuitively, the ELBO balances two competing objectives. The first term encourages qϕ​(z)q_{\phi}(z) to assign high probability to latent variables zz that explain the observed data yy well. The second term acts as a regularizer, penalizing complexity in the approximate posterior by keeping it close to the prior.

To see why the ELBO serves as a lower bound on log⁡p⁡(y)\log p(y), we note the identity:

logp(y)=ℒ(ϕ)+KL(qϕ(z)∥p(z∣y)),\log p(y)=\mathcal{L}(\phi)+\mathrm{KL}\left(q_{\phi}(z)\|p(z\mid y)\right), (11)

which shows that maximizing the ELBO is equivalent to minimizing the divergence from the true posterior. Since the KL divergence is always nonnegative, it follows that log⁡p⁡(y)≥ℒ⁡(ϕ)\log p(y)\geq\mathcal{L}(\phi).

In practice, the approximate posterior qϕ​(z)q_{\phi}(z) is often chosen from a parametric family such as multivariate Gaussians with diagonal covariance, which allows reparameterization techniques and gradient-based optimization. For a comprehensive treatment of variational inference and its theoretical foundations, see [6].

The choice of prior p⁡(z)p(z) plays an important role in variational inference. In many applications, a standard Gaussian prior p⁡(z)=𝒩⁡(0,I)p(z)=\mathcal{N}(0,I) is used due to its simplicity and analytical tractability. Alternative priors, such as Laplace distributions for inducing sparsity or hierarchical priors for modeling structured uncertainty, can be used when specific inductive biases are desired.

2.5 Uncertainty Quantification Metrics

The two main types of uncertainty in uncertainty quantification are aleatoric uncertainty and epistemic uncertainty [24]. Aleatoric uncertainty arises from inherent data or environmental randomness, such as sensor noise or measurement variability, and is therefore irreducible. In contrast, epistemic uncertainty comes from limited data or an incomplete model and is reducible through increased data or refined modeling. In machine learning, aleatoric uncertainty manifests as output ambiguity, whereas epistemic uncertainty reflects model confidence given data limitations [42].

For a node classification task on a graph with nn nodes, CC classes, and an ensemble of TT stochastic forward passes, each input xx yields TT probability vectors pt​(y|x)p_{t}(y|x), where t=1,…,Tt=1,\ldots,T. The ensemble predictive distribution is obtained by averaging the predictions: p¯​(y∣x)=1T​∑t=1Tpt​(y∣x)\bar{p}(y\mid x)=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}p_{t}(y\mid x). The predicted class y^\hat{y} is the class with the highest mean probability, given by y^=arg⁡maxy​p¯​(y∣x)\hat{y}=\arg\max_{y}\bar{p}(y\mid x), and the associated confidence is p^=maxy⁡p¯​(y∣x)\hat{p}=\max_{y}\bar{p}(y\mid x). The variance across ensemble predictions for each class c∈{1,…,C}c\in\{1,\ldots,C\} captures the model’s epistemic uncertainty, and is given by Varc​(x)=Vart=1T​[pt​(y=c∣x)].\text{Var}_{c}(x)=\text{Var}_{t=1}^{T}\left[p_{t}(y=c\mid x)\right]. Several uncertainty qualification metrics can be defined as follows.

Predictive entropy measures the total uncertainty in a model’s output (both aleatoric and epistemic). Lower entropy indicates that the model is more confident in its predictions [33].

H[p¯(y|x)]=−∑c=1Cp¯(y=c∣x)logp¯(y=c∣x).H[\bar{p}(y|x)]=-\sum_{c=1}^{C}\bar{p}(y=c\mid x)\log\bar{p}(y=c\mid x). (12)

Epistemic variance measures the variability in model predictions due to uncertainty in model parameters. Lower epistemic variance implies that the model’s predictions are consistent across stochastic forward passes [49].

EpistemicVariance​(x)=1C​∑c=1CVarc​(x).\text{EpistemicVariance}(x)=\frac{1}{C}\sum_{c=1}^{C}\text{Var}_{c}(x). (13)

Mutual information (MI) quantifies the epistemic component of uncertainty by measuring the divergence between the entropy of the mean prediction and the mean of the individual entropies. Lower MI values indicate reduced epistemic uncertainty, suggesting strong agreement among ensemble members and greater confidence in the model’s parameters [46].

MI​(x)=H⁡[p¯​(y|x)]−1T​∑t=1TH⁡[pt​(y|x)].\text{MI}(x)=H\left[\bar{p}(y|x)\right]-\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}H\left[p_{t}(y|x)\right]. (14)

Expected Calibration Error (ECE) measures the discrepancy between predicted confidence scores and actual accuracy across a range of confidence intervals. To compute the ECE, the prediction confidences p^i\hat{p}_{i} are partitioned into MM equally spaced confidence intervals Im=(m−1M,mM]I_{m}=\left(\frac{m-1}{M},\frac{m}{M}\right] for m=1,…,Mm=1,\dots,M. Let Bm={i∈{1,…,N}|p^i∈Im}B_{m}=\left\{i\in\{1,\dots,N\}\,\middle|\,\hat{p}_{i}\in I_{m}\right\} be the set of indices of samples whose confidence scores fall into interval ImI_{m}.

The accuracy of bin BmB_{m} is defined as the proportion of correctly classified samples in that bin: acc​(Bm)=1|Bm|​∑i∈Bm𝟙​(y^i=yi),\text{acc}(B_{m})=\frac{1}{|B_{m}|}\sum_{i\in B_{m}}\mathbbm{1}(\hat{y}_{i}=y_{i}), and the average confidence is conf​(Bm)=1|Bm|​∑i∈Bmp^i.\text{conf}(B_{m})=\frac{1}{|B_{m}|}\sum_{i\in B_{m}}\hat{p}_{i}.

The Expected Calibration Error is computed as:

ECE=∑m=1M|Bm|N​|acc​(Bm)−conf​(Bm)|.\text{ECE}=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\frac{|B_{m}|}{N}\left|\text{acc}(B_{m})-\text{conf}(B_{m})\right|. (15)

A lower ECE value indicates better calibration, meaning the predicted probabilities are more aligned with the observed accuracy [36].

3 Bayesian Sheaf Neural Networks

In this section, we introduce a Bayesian framework for Sheaf Neural Networks, extending the deterministic architecture by incorporating uncertainty in the learned sheaf structure.

3.1 Problem Statement

Consider a semi-supervised node classification problem, in which we have a graph dataset G=(V,E)G=(V,E) together with a node feature matrix XX, a collection of observed node labels, yy, and a collection of unobserved node labels, y∗y^{*}, all of which are random samples. We model the conditional probability pθ​(y|X)p_{\theta}(y|X) using a sheaf neural network whose layers are given by Eq.(3), with network parameters θ\theta, adjacency matrix AA, and a cellular sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F}.

Rather than taking the learned cellular sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} to be a deterministic function of XX , we regard ℱ\mathcal{F} as a latent random variable of our model. See Figure 1 for a depiction of the probability graphical model. Note that the posterior distribution pθ​(ℱ|X,y)p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) will be intractable due to the fact that the labels yy are modeled as the output of a neural network.

To approximate posterior inference of ℱ\mathcal{F} given the feature matrix XX, the observed node labels yy, and model parameters θ\theta, we assume that the intractable posterior distribution pθ​(ℱ|X,y)p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) belongs to a predetermined family of variational distributions qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) parameterized by weights ϕ\phi as discussed in Section 2.4. In our framework, we choose priors for ℱ\mathcal{F} that reflect plausible variability in sheaf structures while preserving the tractability of inference.

Following Eq.(11), the log-likelihood log⁡pθ​(X,y)\log p_{\theta}(X,y) can be written

logpθ(X,y)=KL(qϕ(ℱ|X,y)∥pθ(ℱ|X,y))+ℒ(θ,ϕ;X,y),\log p_{\theta}(X,y)=\textnormal{KL}(q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)\;\|\;p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}|X,y))+\mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;X,y), (16)

where

ℒ⁡(θ,ϕ,X,y):=𝔼qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)​[−log⁡qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)+log⁡pθ​(ℱ,X,y)].\mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;X,y):=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)}\big[-\log q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)+\log p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F},X,y)\big]. (17)

In order to maximize ℒ⁡(θ,ϕ,X,y)\mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;X,y) with respect to the parameters θ,ϕ\theta,\phi, we use the following equivalent expression:

ℒ(θ,ϕ;X,y)=𝔼qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)[logpθ(X,y|ℱ)]−KL(qϕ(ℱ|X,y)∥pθ(ℱ)).\mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;X,y)=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)}\big[\log p_{\theta}(X,y|\mathcal{F})\big]-\textnormal{KL}(q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)\;\|\;p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F})). (18)

In many cases, a closed-form expression can be derived for the KL divergence term in the right hand side of Eq.(18), leaving only the gradient of the expectation term with respect to θ\theta and ϕ\phi to be estimated. See Appendix Appendix C: KL Divergence Calculations for calculations of the KL divergence in certain cases.

Similar to [47], we estimate ∇ϕ𝔼qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)​[log⁡pθ​(X,y|ℱ)]\nabla_{\phi}\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)}[\log p_{\theta}(X,y|\mathcal{F})] by making use of the so-called reparameterization trick. In our case, for a random cellular sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} distributed as ℱ∼qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)\mathcal{F}\sim q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y), the reparameterization trick expresses ℱ\mathcal{F} as a deterministic function ℱ=gϕ​(ϵ,X)\mathcal{F}=g_{\phi}(\epsilon,X) of random noise ϵ∼p⁡(ϵ)\epsilon\sim p(\epsilon). This allows us to rewrite the expectation with respect to qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) as an expectation with respect to p⁡(ϵ)p(\epsilon) which in turn allows the gradient to be moved within the expectation. That is,

∇ϕ𝔼qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)​[log⁡pθ​(X,y|ℱ)]\displaystyle\nabla_{\phi}\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)}[\log p_{\theta}(X,y|\mathcal{F})] =∇ϕ𝔼p⁡(ϵ)​[log⁡pθ​(X,y|gϕ​(ϵ,X))]\displaystyle=\nabla_{\phi}\mathbb{E}_{p(\epsilon)}[\log p_{\theta}(X,y|g_{\phi}(\epsilon,X))]
=𝔼p⁡(ϵ)​[∇ϕ​log​pθ​(X,y|gϕ​(ϵ,X))]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p(\epsilon)}[\nabla_{\phi}\log p_{\theta}(X,y|g_{\phi}(\epsilon,X))]
≈1K​∑k=1K∇ϕ​log​pθ​(X,y|gϕ​(ϵ(k),X)),\displaystyle\approx\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\nabla_{\phi}\log p_{\theta}(X,y|g_{\phi}(\epsilon^{(k)},X)),

where ϵ(k)\epsilon^{(k)} are independent and identically distributed samples of p⁡(ϵ)p(\epsilon) for k∈{1,2,…,K}k\in\{1,2,\dots,K\}.

Hence, when the KL divergence term of Eq.(18) can be computed analytically, if ℱ(k)=gϕ​(ϵ(k),X)\mathcal{F}^{(k)}=g_{\phi}(\epsilon^{(k)},X) for ϵ(k)∼p⁡(ϵ)\epsilon^{(k)}\sim p(\epsilon), our estimator is

ℒ~λ(θ,ϕ;X,y)=1K∑k=1Klogpθ(X,y|ℱ(k))−λKL(qϕ(ℱ|X,y)∥pθ(ℱ)).\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\lambda}(\theta,\phi;X,y)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\log p_{\theta}(X,y|\mathcal{F}^{(k)})-\lambda\,\textnormal{KL}(q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)\;\|\;p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F})). (19)

Here, the weight λ\lambda of the KL divergence term is included to combat issues with the KL divergence term vanishing during training, which we cyclically anneal during training in a manner similar to [31]. When the KL divergence term of Eq.(18) cannot be computed analytically, we may estimate it in a similar manner by noting that KL(qϕ(ℱ|X,y)∥pθ(ℱ))=𝔼qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)[log(qϕ(ℱ|X,y)/pθ(ℱ))]\textnormal{KL}(q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)\;\|\;p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}))=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)}[\log(q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)/p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}))]. In this case, the estimator, also denoted by ℒ~λ\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\lambda}, is given by

ℒ~λ​(θ,ϕ,X,y)=1K​∑k=1K(log⁡pθ​(X,y|ℱ(k))−λ​log⁡qϕ​(ℱ(k)|X,y)pθ​(ℱ(k))),\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\lambda}(\theta,\phi;X,y)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\Big(\log p_{\theta}(X,y|\mathcal{F}^{(k)})-\lambda\log\frac{q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}^{(k)}|X,y)}{p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}^{(k)})}\Big), (20)

where again, ℱ(k)=gϕ​(ϵ(k),X)\mathcal{F}^{(k)}=g_{\phi}(\epsilon^{(k)},X) for ϵ(k)∼p⁡(ϵ)\epsilon^{(k)}\sim p(\epsilon).

3.2 Variational Sheaf Learner

We make the simplifying assumption that the variational distribution qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) from the previous section factors as the product ∏u​⊴​eqϕ​(ℱu​⊴​e|X,y)\prod_{u\trianglelefteq e}q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}|X,y) over all incident node-edge pairs u​⊴​eu\trianglelefteq e. While this assumption somewhat restricts the family of variational distributions, it makes computing the KL divergence term in the ELBO tractable. For further details, see Appendix Appendix C: KL Divergence Calculations.

We take each factor qϕ​(ℱu​⊴​e|X,y)q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}|X,y) to be a distribution Q⁡(μu​⊴​e,σu​⊴​e)Q(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}) which depends on the type of restriction map used within the sheaf, where the distributional parameters μu​⊴​e,σu​⊴​e\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e} are a function of the node features XX and ϕ\phi as follows. For each incident node-edge pair u​⊴​eu\trianglelefteq e, if u′​⊴​eu^{\prime}\trianglelefteq e denotes the other node incident with ee, a multi-layer perceptron with learned weights ϕ\phi, denoted MLPϕ\MLP_{\phi}, maps the concatenated vector [xu||xu′][x_{u}||x_{u^{\prime}}] to distributional parameters μu​⊴​e\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e} and σu​⊴​e\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}:

[μu​⊴​e||σu​⊴​e]=MLPϕ([xu||xu′]).[\,\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e}\,||\,\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}\,]=\MLP_{\phi}([x_{u}||x_{u^{\prime}}]). (21)

Recall that a multi-layer perceptron is the composition of several feed-forward layers, each of which is a function of the form x↦σ⁡(W​x+b)x\mapsto\sigma(Wx+b), where σ\sigma is a nonlinear activation function, in our case the exponential linear unit (ELU) [20], WW is a weight matrix, and bb is a vector of biases.

The distribution QQ for the variational sheaf learners is considered in three settings, where the learned sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} has restriction maps assumed to be: (1) general linear, (2) invertible diagonal, or (3) special orthogonal.

Case 1: General Linear. In the case where the sheaf restriction maps ℱu​⊴​e:ℱ⁡(u)→ℱ⁡(e)\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}:\mathcal{F}(u)\to\mathcal{F}(e) are general linear maps, μu​⊴​e\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e} and σu​⊴​e\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e} are d2d^{2}−-dimensional vectors. We take Q⁡(μu​⊴​e,σu​⊴​e)Q(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}) to be normal with diagonal covariance so that for z∼𝒩d2​(μu​⊴​e,diag⁡(σu​⊴​e))z\sim\mathcal{N}_{d^{2}}(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\diag(\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e})) we set ℱu​⊴​e\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e} to be the vector zz rearranged into a d×dd\times d matrix. The reparameterization trick in this case writes z=μu​⊴​e+diag⁡(σu​⊴​e)​ϵz=\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e}+\diag(\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e})\epsilon for ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,Id2)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},I_{d^{2}}) so that ℱu​⊴​e\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}, being the matrix obtained by reshaping the vector zz, is a deterministic function of μu​⊴​e\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e}, σu​⊴​e\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}, and ϵ\epsilon. We use a standard normal prior, where pθ​(ℱ)=∏u​⊴​epθ​(ℱu​⊴​e)p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F})=\prod_{u\trianglelefteq e}p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}) and pθ​(ℱu​⊴​e)=𝒩d2​(𝟎,Id2)p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e})=\mathcal{N}_{d^{2}}(\mathbf{0},I_{d^{2}}).

Case 2: Invertible Diagonal. In the case where sheaf restriction maps ℱu​⊴​e\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e} are assumed to be invertible diagonal matrices with respect to the standard basis, μu​⊴​e\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e} and σu​⊴​e\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e} are dd−-dimensional vectors and we take qϕ​(ℱu​⊴​e|X,y)=Q⁡(μu​⊴​e,σu​⊴​e)q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}|X,y)=Q(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}) to be a normal distribution with diagonal covariance, so that ℱu​⊴​e=diag⁡(z)\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}=\diag(z) for z∼𝒩d​(μu​⊴​e,diag⁡(σu​⊴​e))z\sim\mathcal{N}_{d}(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\diag(\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e})). The reparameterization ℱ=gϕ​(X,ϵ)\mathcal{F}=g_{\phi}(X,\epsilon) in this case is given by setting ℱu​⊴​e=diag⁡(μu​⊴​e+σu​⊴​e​ϵ)\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}=\diag(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e}+\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}\epsilon) for ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,Id)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},I_{d}). Lastly, we use a standard normal prior, where pθ​(ℱ)=∏u​⊴​epθ​(ℱu​⊴​e)p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F})=\prod_{u\trianglelefteq e}p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}) and pθ​(ℱu​⊴​e)=𝒩d​(𝟎,Id)p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e})=\mathcal{N}_{d}(\mathbf{0},I_{d}).

Case 3: Special Orthogonal. The class of sheaves with special orthogonal restriction maps is of particular interest for sheaf neural networks, including our Bayesian sheaf neural networks, due to both theoretical and practical properties. From a theoretical point of view, certain results concerning the kernel of Δℱ\Delta_{\mathcal{F}} can be proven for sheaves using rotations as restriction maps [10, Section 3.1]. Regarding the more practical aspects, rotations offer a nice middle-ground between diagonal and general linear maps in terms of balancing the number of parameters with the expressivity of the resulting sheaf. Moreover, when using rotations, the blocks along the diagonal of the sheaf Laplacian LℱL_{\mathcal{F}} are scalar multiples of the identity matrix. This makes computing the normalized sheaf Laplacian Δℱ\Delta_{\mathcal{F}} easier.

These properties motivate our focus on S​O​(d)SO(d) sheaves. To further support their utility, we extend previous theoretical results on their separation power as defined in Section 2.2. In particular, we prove that for any number of classes C∈ℕC\in\mathbb{N}, we may find dd large enough such that ℋs​od\mathcal{H}_{so}^{d} has linear separation power over 𝒢C\mathcal{G}_{C}. In the following proposition, ⌊⋅⌋\lfloor\cdot\rfloor denotes the floor function.

Proposition 1.

For any d≥1d\geq 1, if 𝒢\mathcal{G} denotes the class of connected graphs with C≤7​⌊d4⌋C\leq 7\lfloor\tfrac{d}{4}\rfloor classes, then ℋs​od\mathcal{H}_{so}^{d} has linear separation power over 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

For a proof see Appendix Appendix A: Proof of Proposition .

Remark 6.

An extra consequence of Proposition 1 is that it also provides a new upper bound on the stalk dimension dd necessary for ℋg​e​nd\mathcal{H}^{d}_{gen}, the collection of sheaves with d×dd\times d general linear restriction maps, to have linear separation power over the collection of connected graph 𝒢C\mathcal{G}_{C} with CC classes. This is due to the simple fact that ℋs​od⊆ℋg​e​nd\mathcal{H}^{d}_{so}\subseteq\mathcal{H}^{d}_{gen}.

We now turn to the practical challenge of incorporating these S​O​(d)SO(d) maps into the variational model. Typical probability distributions on S​O​(d)SO(d), such as the matrix Langevin distribution, are not easily reparameterizable. This makes incorporating such distributions into neural networks that are trained via back-propagation difficult. On the other hand, while reparameterizable distributions on S​O​(d)SO(d) have been constructed in [27] using the exponential map, the density functions of such distributions can be difficult to compute exactly, which obstructs one from computing, or even efficiently estimating, the KL divergence term in Eq.(18).

In Section 3.3, we introduce Cayley distributions, a family of reparameterizable distributions 𝒞d​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{d}(M,\kappa) on S​O​(d)SO(d) with closed form expressions for their probability density functions. We use 𝒞d​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{d}(M,\kappa) as the variational distributions for sheaves with special orthogonal restriction maps. Hence when ℱu​⊴​e∈S​O​(d)\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}\in SO(d), the distributional parameters are a mean rotation μu​⊴​e∈S​O​(d)\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e}\in SO(d) and scalar concentration parameter σu​⊴​e∈[0,1)\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}\in[0,1), and we have Q⁡(μu​⊴​e,σu​⊴​e)=𝒞d​(μu​⊴​e,σu​⊴​e)Q(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e})=\mathcal{C}_{d}(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}). The reparameterization of the Cayley distributions is described in Remark 7. We use a prior distribution pθ​(ℱ)=∏u​⊴​epθ​(ℱu​⊴​e)p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F})=\prod_{u\trianglelefteq e}p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}) where each pθ​(ℱu​⊴​e)p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}) is a uniform distribution on S​O​(d)SO(d).

3.3 Cayley Distributions on S​O​(n)SO(n)

To enable reparameterizable inference on S​O​(n)SO(n), we define a novel family of distributions using the Cayley transform.

Definition 8.

Let C:𝔰​𝔬​(n)→S​O​(n)C:\mathfrak{so}(n)\to SO(n) denote the Cayley transform and let XX be a uniformly distributed random variable on S​O​(n)SO(n). Given parameters M∈S​O​(n)M\in SO(n) and 0≤κ<10\leq\kappa<1, we define the Cayley distribution 𝒞n​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{n}(M,\kappa) on S​O​(n)SO(n) inspired by the constructions in [50] to be the distribution of Y=C⁡(1−κ1+κ​C−1​(X))​MY=C\left(\frac{1-\kappa}{1+\kappa}C^{-1}(X)\right)M.

Remark 7.

Note that by the definition of the Cayley distribution, a random variable Y∼𝒞n​(M,κ)Y\sim\mathcal{C}_{n}(M,\kappa) can be expressed as a deterministic function of MM, κ\kappa, and X∼US​O​(n)X\sim U_{SO(n)}. Hence these distributions are theoretically reparameterizable. For details on sampling from the uniform distribution on S​O​(n)SO(n), see for example [2].

In order to compute or efficiently estimate the KL divergence term in Eq.(19), an expression for the density of 𝒞n​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{n}(M,\kappa) is necessary. Using Eq.(6) for the Jacobian of the Cayley transform, we compute the density of 𝒞n​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{n}(M,\kappa) in the following theorem.

Theorem 1.

Let P∈S​O​(n)P\in SO(n), the Cayley distribution 𝒞n​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{n}(M,\kappa) has density

fn​(P,M,κ)=(1−κ2)n⁡(n−1)2​det(P​M𝖳−κ​I)1−n,f_{n}(P;M,\kappa)=(1-\kappa^{2})^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}\det\Big(PM^{\mathsf{T}}-\kappa I\Big)^{1-n}, (22)

with respect to the normalized Haar measure on S​O​(n)SO(n).

For a proof see Appendix Appendix B: Section Proofs.

Remark 8.

The family of Cayley distributions defined in [50] have density proportional to det(P​M𝖳+I)κ\det(PM^{\mathsf{T}}+I)^{\kappa} of Eq.(22). Note that the concentration parameter κ\kappa appears in the exponent of the determinant expression, whereas in our proposed family of Cayley distributions, κ\kappa instead scales the identity matrix term within the determinant. This structural difference plays a key role in enabling reparameterizable constructions based on the Cayley transform, particularly in low dimensions.

For small values of n,n, the structure of S​O​(n)SO(n) allows for simpler parameterizations and more efficient sampling schemes. We now examine these cases to motivate practical approaches for facilitating differentiable sampling from 𝒞n​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{n}(M,\kappa).

Case 𝐧=𝟐\mathbf{n=2}. If P,M∈S​O​(2)P,M\in SO(2) are rotations by θ,μ\theta,\mu radians respectively, then 𝒞2​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{2}(M,\kappa) has density

f2​(P,M,κ)=12​π⋅1−κ21+κ2−2​κ​cos⁡(θ−μ).f_{2}(P;M,\kappa)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{1-\kappa^{2}}{1+\kappa^{2}-2\kappa\cos(\theta-\mu)}.

This is the density of a wrapped Cauchy distribution on S​O​(2)≅S1SO(2)\cong S^{1}, see [45]. Hence for the case n=2n=2, the Cayley distributions coincide with known distributions.

Case 𝐧=𝟑\mathbf{n=3}. Note that S​O​(3)SO(3) is homeomorphic to 33−-dimensional real projective space R​P3RP^{3}, which is the quotient of S3S^{3} under the identification of antipodal points. We show that 𝒞3​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{3}(M,\kappa) is related to an angular central Gaussian distribution [61] on S3S^{3}. Specifically, we show that 𝒞3​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{3}(M,\kappa) is the pushforward of an angular central Gaussian distribution on S3S^{3} under the quotient map Φ:S3→S​O​(3)\Phi:S^{3}\to SO(3). This provides a reparameterizable sampling strategy, distinct from sampling via uniform S​O​(3)SO(3).

If x∈ℝn+1x\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1} is a unit vector, Λ∈ℝ(n+1)×(n+1)\Lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{(n+1)\times(n+1)} is a symmetric positive definite matrix, and αn\alpha_{n} denotes the volume of the nn−-dimensional sphere SnS^{n}, the angular central Gaussian distribution A​C​Gn​(Λ)ACG_{n}(\Lambda) on SnS^{n} has density

f⁡(x,Λ)=αn−1​det(Λ)−12​(x𝖳​Λ−1​x)−2,f(x;\Lambda)=\alpha_{n}^{-1}\det(\Lambda)^{-\frac{1}{2}}(x^{\mathsf{T}}\Lambda^{-1}x)^{-2},

with respect to the uniform measure on SnS^{n}.

Proposition 2.

Let Φ:S3→ℝ​ℙ3≅S​O​(3)\Phi:S^{3}\to\mathbb{R}\mathbb{P}^{3}\cong SO(3) denote the map which identifies antipodal points of S3S^{3}. For any M∈S​O​(3)M\in SO(3) and κ∈[0,1)\kappa\in[0,1), there exists a symmetric positive definite matrix ΛM,κ∈ℝ4×4\Lambda_{M,\kappa}\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times 4} such that if X∼A​C​G3​(ΛM,κ)X\sim ACG_{3}(\Lambda_{M,\kappa}), then Φ⁡(X)∼𝒞3​(M,κ)\Phi(X)\sim\mathcal{C}_{3}(M,\kappa).

For a proof see Appendix Appendix B: Section Proofs.

When n=2n=2 or n=3n=3, Eq.(6) for the Jacobian of the Cayley transform simplifies to 23​n​(n−1)/4​(1+‖ϕ‖2)1−n2^{3n(n-1)/4}(1+\|\phi\|^{2})^{1-n}. One consequence of this fact is that 𝒞n​(In,κ)\mathcal{C}_{n}(I_{n},\kappa) is the pushforward of a Cauchy distribution (multivariate in the case n=3n=3) under the Cayley transform. This fact makes it possible to compute the KL divergence of 𝒞n​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{n}(M,\kappa) from the uniform distribution on S​O​(n)SO(n) in these cases. Note that while the prior is uniform on S​O​(n)SO(n), reparameterizable sampling is achieved via Cauchy or A​C​G3ACG_{3} distributions in latent space.

Proposition 3.

For n=2,3n=2,3 the KL divergence of 𝒞n​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{n}(M,\kappa) from the uniform distribution is given by

KL(𝒞2(M,κ)∥US​O​(2))\displaystyle\textnormal{KL}(\mathcal{C}_{2}(M,\kappa)\;\|\;U_{SO(2)}) =−log⁡(1−κ2)\displaystyle=-\log(1-\kappa^{2})
KL(𝒞3(M,κ)∥US​O​(3))\displaystyle\textnormal{KL}(\mathcal{C}_{3}(M,\kappa)\;\|\;U_{SO(3)}) =−log⁡(1−κ2)−2​log⁡(1−κ)−2​κ.\displaystyle=-\log(1-\kappa^{2})-2\log(1-\kappa)-2\kappa.

For a proof see Appendix Appendix C: KL Divergence Calculations.

Thus when learning a distribution of cellular sheaves with special orthogonal restriction maps in our BSNN, for the cases where the stalk dimension dd is 22 or 33, we are able to use Eq.(19) to estimate the ELBO by plugging in the expressions for the KL divergence from Proposition 3. When d≥4d\geq 4, we estimate the ELBO by simply using Eq.(20).

3.4 Bayesian Sheaf Neural Network Architecture

We present the Bayesian sheaf neural network architecture, which is also summarized in Figure 2 and Algorithm 1. The variational sheaf learning mechanism maps the input node features to the sheaf distributional parameters as described in Section 3.2, For completeness, we briefly review the mechanism here as well.

A linear layer first resizes the input node features to dimension kk. Specifically, we use k=d​fk=df where dd and ff are the stalk dimensions and number of feature channels respectively. For each edge e=(u,u′)∈Ee=(u,u^{\prime})\in E, we consider the two incident node-edge pairs u​⊴​eu\trianglelefteq e and u′​⊴​eu^{\prime}\trianglelefteq e. For each pair, we construct a feature vector by concatenating the features of the node with those of the node at the other end of the edge. Hence, a node feature matrix of size n×kn\times k is transformed by this concatenation operation into a matrix of size 2​e×2​k2e\times 2k, where nn denotes the number of nodes, and ee denotes the number of edges in the graph.

Lastly, an MLP maps these features indexed by the incident node-edge pairs u​⊴​eu\trianglelefteq e to distributional parameters μu​⊴​e\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e} and σu​⊴​e\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e} as described by Eq.(21), which define the distribution over the cellular sheaves. From this distribution, a collection of independent and identically distributed sheaves ℱ1,ℱ2,…,ℱL\mathcal{F}_{1},\mathcal{F}_{2},\dots,\mathcal{F}_{L} are sampled: one for each layer of the network.

Separately, a multi-layer perceptron maps the input node features X∈ℝn×mX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} to features of dimension X′∈ℝn×d​fX^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times df} where dd is the stalk dimension and ff is the number of hidden channels. The features X′X^{\prime} are reshaped to size n​d×fnd\times f.

Sheaf layers described by Eq.(3) update the transformed features X′X^{\prime} using the sampled sheaves ℱ1,ℱ2,…,ℱL\mathcal{F}_{1},\mathcal{F}_{2},\dots,\mathcal{F}_{L}. Finally, a linear layer maps the output of the final sheaf layer to a vector of class probabilities.

During training, a one-sample Monte Carlo estimate of Eq.(19) or Eq.(20) is computed, and the loss is back-propagated to update the network weights. During testing, multiple sheaf samples are drawn from the learned posterior, and ensembling is performed over the corresponding forward passes to obtain point estimates for the unobserved node labels y∗y^{*}.

4 Experiments and Uncertainty Quantification

We compare our proposed model against a comprehensive set of baseline methods, including classical and advanced graph neural networks (GNNs), and modern deep geometric learning architectures.

4.1 Results

Sheaf neural networks are expected to outperform traditional graph neural networks on datasets with low edge-homophily coefficients, that is, datasets where relatively few edges connect nodes belonging to the same class [69].

We evaluate our model using the NSD benchmark [10], which compiles standardized results across datasets with varying levels of homophily, from low (Texas) to high (Cora), enabling fair and diverse comparison. For more details on the datasets, see Appendix Appendix D: Experiment Details.

Baselines include standard GNNs designed for homophilic settings (GCN [48], GAT [62], GraphSAGE [38]), models tailored for heterophilic graphs (GGCN [63], Geom-GCN [57], H2GCN [69], GPRGNN [17], MixHop [1]), and architectures addressing oversmoothing (GCNII [16], PairNorm [68]). Most results are sourced from [63], with MixHop from [7] and [69].

All models, including ours, are evaluated on 10 fixed splits comprising 48% training, 32% validation, and 20% testing data. We report mean accuracy and standard deviation across these splits. Model configurations are selected via random hyperparameter search, with test results reported at the epoch yielding the best validation performance (see Appendix Appendix D: Experiment Details Table 7 for the full hyperparameter list). The final model is chosen based on the highest validation score across all candidates.

The results in Table 1 demonstrate that the BSNN models consistently attain peak or near-peak test accuracies across a wide range of datasets. On heterophilic datasets such as Texas and Wisconsin, BSNN variants are competitive with state-of-the-art methods, with accuracies reaching 88.11% on Texas and 89.80% on Wisconsin. Similarly, on homophilic benchmarks such as Pubmed and Cora, BSNN variants match or slightly exceed advanced methods, achieving 89.66% and 87.53% accuracy, respectively. These results indicate that BSNN models are robust to varying degrees of homophily and generalize effectively across different graph structures.

Notably, on the challenging Film dataset with low homophily, sparse connectivity, and high label noise, BSNN models achieve test accuracy comparable to leading methods, indicating robustness to noisy and weakly informative graph structures.

Overall, these results demonstrate that the incorporation of Bayesian uncertainty modeling into graph neural networks provides significant benefits across a broad spectrum of datasets.

4.2 Uncertainty Quantification

Given that BSNN models learn predictive distributions on sheaves, we evaluate their reliability, and calibration using metrics such as entropy, epistemic variance, mutual information, and expected calibration error as outlined in Section 2.5. We conduct independent training trials using 30 random seeds with the best hyperparameter configuration, namely the one that achieved the highest validation accuracy. For each trial, a BSNN model samples a new sheaf instance and performs three forward passes. We use these predictions to compute node-wise uncertainty statistics.

For each test node, we calculate entropy to quantify total uncertainty, and estimate epistemic variance to capture model uncertainty. As shown in Figure 3, epistemic variance is more sensitive to model choice than entropy. This variability in epistemic uncertainty across models is natural and expected, as different models embody distinct prior beliefs and architectures, which interact with datasets in different ways. In contrast, entropy remains relatively stable across models for a given dataset, suggesting that it is likely dominated by aleatoric uncertainty.

Most nodes exhibit low epistemic variance (near 0) and low to moderate entropy, suggesting that models are generally confident and consistent in their predictions, with no clear correlation between epistemic variance and homophily level across models. The maximum observed epistemic variance (0.08) is on Cornell when Gen-BSNN is used, while the rest of the plots show a maximum epistemic variance of about 0.04. Node degree does not appear to significantly influence epistemic variance, as Citeseer and Film both exhibit low variance under Gen-BSNN despite having markedly different average degrees, where Citeseer being sparsely connected and Film more densely connected.

Among the three BSNN variants, Diag-BSNN exhibits lower epistemic variance than Gen-BSNN and S​O​(d)SO(d)-BSNN in most datasets. This suggests that its simplified diagonal posterior often leads to more conservative uncertainty estimates, but its behavior still varies depending on the specific dataset characteristics.

In most datasets, models demonstrate confident predictions for the majority of nodes, as indicated by a high concentration of low-entropy values. Only a smaller subset of nodes shows elevated entropy and variability, which typically points to localized uncertainty arising from ambiguous features. In contrast, the Film dataset shows more consistent entropy levels across nodes, with overall low variance, suggesting that the observed uncertainty is likely due to noise rather than informative structure. This interpretation is supported by the low mutual information (MI) values, as will be shown in Figure 4.

Table 2 presents average uncertainty scores, computed by first averaging predictive entropy and epistemic variance within each dataset, and then averaging those values across all datasets. The observed averages suggest that all models are similarly confident with moderately low uncertainty overall.

Since predictive entropy is nearly invariant across models, we compute mutual information (MI) to better capture differences in uncertainty. The histograms that illustrate mutual information in Figure 4 are heavily skewed toward 1.0 across all datasets and all models. This suggests that the BSNN models are very confident about most of their predictions. As for Cornell, a small proportion of samples have a higher MI, meaning the model is uncertain about these specific samples, likely due to out-of-distribution features, or decision boundary proximity. This is not surprising, as these samples also exhibited the highest epistemic uncertainty, further indicating the model’s lack of confidence in its predictions for these cases.

We compute the Expected Calibration Error (ECE) to assess the alignment between predicted confidence and actual accuracy, and report the results in Table 3. On datasets with high homophily levels, the ECE values that are below 0.1 show that the predicted probabilities closely align with actual outcomes, and that the models are well-calibrated. In contrast, on heterophilic datasets such as Texas, Wisconsin, and Film, the ECE values are higher. This suggests that while the models may achieve high accuracy, they are overconfident. To address this, post-hoc calibration techniques such as temperature scaling could be applied to improve the reliability of confidence scores without retraining the model.

4.3 Robustness Under Limited Data

To evaluate the performance of our Bayesian sheaf models under limited training data, we use 10 fixed dataset splits, with each split allocating 32% of the nodes for training, 20% for validation, and 48% for testing. For each model configuration, we report test results from the epoch with the best validation score. The final model is selected as the configuration with the highest validation performance overall. As shown in Table 4, our model still achieves high accuracy in most datasets, even in this low-data regime.

Additionally, to examine the sensitivity of the Bayesian and deterministic sheaf models to the hyperparameter selections, we perform a grid search over selected hyperparameters, as detailed in Appendix Appendix D: Experiment Details, Table 8. We report the mean test accuracy across all hyperparameter configurations in Table 5.

The advantage of each BSNN model over the corresponding NSD model when considering the entire range of hyperparameters is definitive. A Wilcoxon signed-rank test for a pp-value threshold of p=0.05p=0.05 indicates a statistically significant improvement in performance for the Diag-BSNN and Gen-BSNN models over their NSD counterparts across datasets.

Thus, we observe that the BSNN models maintain good performance over a much wider range of hyperparameters when compared with the NSD model with the same type of restriction maps. We also include results for a graph convolutional network (GCN) as a baseline comparison.

5 Conclusion and Future Directions

In this work, we have introduced Bayesian sheaf neural networks: novel sheaf neural networks in which the sheaf Laplacian is a random latent variable, and where the loss function used in training contains a Kullback-Leibler divergence regularization term. Not only does this allow one to quantify uncertainty of the model arising from the learned sheaf, but we show that our BSNN models achieve results that are comparable to, and in some cases exceed, state-of-the-art node classification methods. Furthermore, our experiments suggest that the BSNN models are more robust to different choices of hyperparameters and weight initializations, particularly under limited training data, compared to their deterministic counterparts.

We hope that this paper encourages further work on stochastic sheaf neural networks. We briefly mention some possible future directions. Different priors for the distribution of sheaf Laplacians could be suitable for the BSNN depending on the graph dataset, in particular, depending on the level of edge homophily. Although we view the underlying graph as fixed in this paper, one could view it probabilistically and combine our work with the approach taken in [66]. Lastly, similar to the continuous-time version of the sheaf diffusion network that was studied in [10], a continuous-time version of the BSNN could be considered, where the sheaf Laplacian is a stochastic process.

Appendix A: Proof of Proposition 1

Recall that we assume that the variational distribution qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) factors as qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)=∏u​⊴​eqϕ​(ℱu​⊴​e|X,y)q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)=\prod_{u\trianglelefteq e}q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}|X,y) over all incident node-edge pairs u​⊴​eu\trianglelefteq e, and that we use a prior pθ​(ℱ)p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}) which also factors in the same manner pθ​(ℱ)=∏u​⊴​epθ​(ℱu​⊴​e)p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F})=\prod_{u\trianglelefteq e}p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}). As a consequence of the chain rule for KL divergence, see for example Theorem 2.5.3 in [22], we have

KL(qϕ(ℱ|X,y)∥pθ(ℱ))=∑u​⊴​eKL(qϕ(ℱu​⊴​e|X,y)∥pθ(ℱu​⊴​e)).\textnormal{KL}(q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)\;\|\;p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}))=\sum_{u\trianglelefteq e}\textnormal{KL}(q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}|X,y)\;\|\;p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e})).

Appendix D: Experiment Details

We selected a diverse set of real-world datasets exhibiting varying levels of homophily. Table 6 shows the number of nodes, edges, and classes in each dataset.

The Texas, Cornell, and Wisconsin datasets are part of the WebKB collection, each representing the computer science department of a respective university. Each dataset is a graph in which nodes represent web pages and edges represent hyperlinks between them. In all datasets the node features are 17031703−-dimensional bag-of-word representations of the web pages.

The Film dataset is a graph of actors, where nodes represent actors and edges represent co-appearances in films. Node features are derived from metadata such as keywords and genres, and each node belongs to one of several genre-based classes.

The Pubmed dataset is a citation network of scientific publications. Each node represents a paper, and edges represent citation links. Node features are TF/IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency) weighted word vectors from the paper abstracts, and nodes are labeled according to their subject area.

The CiteSeer and Cora datasets are also citation networks. Nodes represent documents, and edges indicate citations between them. Node features are bag-of-word vectors, and each document is categorized into a specific topic.

Chameleon and Squirrel, which were included in earlier studies, were excluded from our experiments because they have been removed from the official Geom-GCN repository due to maintenance or quality concerns.

All experiments were run on a computing cluster equipped with an NVIDIA H100 GPU (80GB HBM3), two Intel Xeon Platinum 8462Y+ CPUs, and 1.0 TiB of RAM. The code was implemented in PyTorch and executed using CUDA 12.4 with NVIDIA driver 550.54.15.. Our code is available at https://github.com/Layal-Bou-Hamdan/BSNN.

Hyperparameter tuning was done using Weights & Biases [5]. The full range of hyperparameters that we optimize using random search is listed in Table 7.

To perform a hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, we used the hyperparameters listed in Table 8 with node splits of 32% for training, 20% for validation, and 48% for testing.
